cards.q: In Design Google Drive, where do file bytes go, and where does file info go?
cards.a: Bytes go in **object storage** like S3: cheap, very durable, almost no size limit. File info (metadata) goes in a SQL database split by user ID, because it needs transactions and fast queries. Never put big files in a database.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, what does the quick math say about file data and file info?
cards.a: File data: 100 million users × about 5 GB = **500 PB**, so object storage. File info: 100 million users × 1,000 files × about 1 KB = **100 TB**, too big for one database, so we split it by user ID.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, what is the best way to upload a big file?
cards.a: Cut it into 4 MB chunks. Upload each one straight to storage with **presigned URLs**: our servers only hand out links. Chunks go in parallel. If the network drops, the app uploads only the chunks storage doesn't have yet.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, what two extra wins do chunks named by their hash give?
cards.a: **Upload only what changed:** only chunks with a new hash are sent. **Deduplication:** a chunk already in this account, like in an old version of the same file, is stored once and skipped.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, why do we dedupe chunks only inside one account?
cards.a: Across all users, anyone who only knows a file's hashes could "upload" it without having the bytes, then download the real file. A tool called Dropship did exactly this with Dropbox in 2011.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, how do we stop a buggy app from uploading wrong bytes under a chunk's hash?
cards.a: Storage checks during the upload: the presigned URL requires a SHA-256 checksum equal to the chunk's hash, and storage rejects bytes that don't match. If storage can't, a worker hashes each new chunk before `complete` succeeds.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, how do changes reach a user's other devices?
cards.a: Every change goes into the user's **change log**, and each device keeps a **cursor**. A live nudge (long poll or WebSocket) tells the device to call `/changes` with its cursor. The cursor is the truth, so a missed nudge loses nothing.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, why not just poll for changes every 30 seconds?
cards.a: Changes would arrive up to 30 seconds late, and most calls return nothing. A long poll instead keeps the request open until there is a change, or about a minute passes. It carries the device's cursor, so if the change log is already ahead, it answers at once.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, two devices edit the same file from version 5. Who wins?
cards.a: Each save sends its `baseVersion` (optimistic locking). If that is still the current version, the save wins. If not, the server answers `409 Conflict`, and the app saves a separate "conflicted copy". Nothing is lost.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, why not lock the file, or merge conflicting edits automatically?
cards.a: A lock does not work offline, and people forget to unlock files. Merging is unsafe because most files are binary, like photos, videos and zip files. There is no safe way to merge two photos.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, how does Ben's "Shared with me" list stay a one-shard query?
cards.a: `shares` rows live on the owner's shard, so we also add a `shared_with_me` row split by Ben's user ID. The rows are on different shards, so an outbox event goes through Kafka, and a Share Worker adds Ben's row.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, how do you rename a folder with 10,000 files in it cheaply?
cards.a: Folders point to their parent **by ID**, not by full path. So the rename is a one-row update.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, how does the cleanup job avoid deleting a chunk that a new upload just reused?
cards.a: Both sides change the same `chunks` row with a conditional update, so only one can win. An upload takes a reference only if the chunk is `live`. Cleanup claims it only if `refCount` is 0 and unused for a day. If the chunk is `deleting`, the upload waits until cleanup removes it, then uploads it again.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, `complete` worked but its reply was lost. How does the retry avoid a 409 against its own save?
cards.a: `complete` carries the `uploadId` from `POST /files`, and each version row stores it. When the version check fails, the server first looks for that `uploadId`. Found: it answers `200` with that version again. Not found: it is a real conflict, `409`.

cards.q: In Design Google Drive, what does a save based on version 5 run in the database?
cards.a: One transaction: `UPDATE files SET current_version = current_version + 1 WHERE ... AND current_version = 5`. 0 rows: conflict, roll back. 1 row: insert the `file_versions` row for version 6, plus the change log row and the outbox event.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, what does the quick math say about uploads and watching?
cards.a: Uploads: 1 million × about 1 GB = **1 PB per day**, so object storage. Watching: 10 million viewers × about 5 Mbps = **50 Tbps**. No single data center can send that much, so we must serve video from a **CDN**.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, how does a creator upload a huge video?
cards.a: **Multipart upload with presigned URLs:** split it into parts (say 10 MB) and upload them straight to object storage, several at a time. If the network drops, upload only the missing parts. One S3 request can carry at most 5 GB anyway.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, who joins the uploaded parts, and who starts processing?
cards.a: Storage never joins parts by itself. The app sends the part ETags to `complete`, and the **Video Service** calls `CompleteMultipartUpload`. Only after that succeeds does it mark the video `processing` and start processing.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, what happens if the app retries `complete`, or never calls it?
cards.a: A retry sees the video is already `processing` and answers `202` again. Marking `processing` and writing a "start" outbox row happen in one transaction, so a crash can't leave the video stuck. If `complete` never comes, a storage cleanup rule deletes the parts after a few days.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, how do you transcode a long 4K video in minutes, not hours?
cards.a: One machine could take hours and start over if it dies. Instead, cut the raw video into short pieces (say 10 seconds). Each "transcode piece 7 into 720p" is a small task on a queue for hundreds of workers. A failed task is just retried.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, what does the orchestrator do in the processing pipeline?
cards.a: The steps form a **DAG**: some steps wait for others, and nothing loops back. The orchestrator keeps each task's state in a database, puts ready tasks on the queue, and starts the next step when a step is done.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, how can a new video become watchable before its 4K version is ready?
cards.a: Publish the low qualities first. When 360p and 720p are ready, mark the video watchable. 4K can arrive a little later.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, how does adaptive bitrate streaming keep playback smooth?
cards.a: Each version is cut into small **segments** of a few seconds. Before each segment, the player checks how fast recent downloads were and how much video is in its **buffer**, then picks the best quality the network can handle right now.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, what is the manifest, and what are the two common streaming standards?
cards.a: The manifest is a small text file that lists every quality, its bitrate, and where its segments are. The standards are **HLS** (made by Apple, `.m3u8`) and **MPEG-DASH** (an open standard, `.mpd`).

cards.q: In Design YouTube, why do video segments cache so well on a CDN?
cards.a: Segments never change once made, so edges keep them a long time and never clear them. The master manifest does change (4K is added later), so it gets a short cache time. Popular videos end up on almost every edge. The long tail is served from the origin or regional caches.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, how do you count views for a viral video without a hot database row?
cards.a: One update per view makes every write wait on the same row's lock. Instead, send view events to **Kafka**. Counter workers add up each video's views for about 10 seconds, then write one update like `views = views + 5234`.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, how do counter workers avoid adding a batch twice after a crash?
cards.a: "Add" is not safe to repeat. So save the Kafka offset in the **same database transaction** as the counts. On restart, the worker reads `next_offset` from the database and asks Kafka from there. Each batch is added exactly once.

cards.q: In Design YouTube, why does our API never send video bytes?
cards.a: Uploads go straight to storage with presigned URLs, and the player downloads segments from the CDN using the `manifestUrl`. Our API only handles video info.

cards.q: In Design Uber, what does the quick math say about driver locations?
cards.a: 2 million drivers ÷ 5 seconds = **400,000 updates per second**, far too many writes for a normal database. But 2 million × about 100 bytes is only **200 MB**. So keep live locations **in memory**.

cards.q: In Design Uber, what is the best way to store driver locations?
cards.a: Keep only **where each driver is now**, in a Redis **geo index** split by city. Every update simply replaces the old position. We don't need a history, and Redis handles a huge number of small writes per second.

cards.q: In Design Uber, what happens to driver locations if Redis crashes?
cards.a: We lose almost nothing. Moving drivers send a fresh location every 5 seconds and parked ones every 15, so the index fills itself up again within about 15 seconds. Old positions were never worth saving.

cards.q: In Design Uber, what is a geohash?
cards.a: A way to turn latitude and longitude into **one** code, so a normal sorted index can find everything in a box fast. The map is split into 32 boxes, each into 32 more, and so on. A box's code starts with its parent's code.

cards.q: In Design Uber, why search the pickup's geohash box plus the 8 boxes around it?
cards.a: Two drivers can be 10 meters apart but on opposite sides of a box border, so their codes differ. The box must be at least as big as the search radius, and then we drop drivers farther than the radius. Redis `GEOSEARCH` does both for us.

cards.q: In Design Uber, why is PostGIS only "okay" for finding nearby drivers, and what is best?
cards.a: PostGIS gives fast location queries, but it is a disk-based database and can't take 400,000 updates per second. Best is **Redis GEO**: a sorted set with a geohash as the score, searched in well under a millisecond.

cards.q: In Design Uber, why rank nearby drivers by driving time, not distance?
cards.a: A driver 300 meters away on the other side of a river may need 15 minutes. So take the 10 closest drivers, ask the Maps API for each one's real driving time (ETA), and offer the ride to the best one.

cards.q: In Design Uber, why is "check the driver's status, then send the offer" wrong?
cards.a: Two servers can both read "driver 42 is available" at the same moment, and both send an offer. This race condition gives driver 42 two rides.

cards.q: In Design Uber, how do you make sure only one server offers a ride to driver 42?
cards.a: Take a Redis lock first: `SET lock:driver:42 ride_789 NX EX 10`. `NX` lets only one server get it. `EX 10` makes it disappear after 10 seconds, so a driver who doesn't answer is free for the next offer.

cards.q: In Design Uber, what must be checked when a driver accepts a ride?
cards.a: The lock must still hold this ride. Then one transaction with two conditional updates: the ride must still be `matching`, and the driver must still be `available`. If either changes 0 rows, roll back: the ride is gone.

cards.q: In Design Uber, why can't the Redis lock be the final guard against double booking?
cards.a: The lock only decides who gets the offer, and it can expire between the check and the database write. The two conditional updates in the Rides DB make sure a ride gets one driver and a driver gets one ride.

cards.q: In Design Uber, why does `POST /rides` carry an `Idempotency-Key`?
cards.a: Phones often lose the network for a moment. Without the key, a retry would create a second ride, and two drivers would drive to the same rider. With it, the Ride Service sees the saved key and returns the first ride.

cards.q: In Design Uber, how do you handle busy peaks like New Year's Eve?
cards.a: **Split by city**, each with its own Redis shard. Put ride requests in **Kafka**, split by region, so the queue gets longer instead of dropping requests. **Raise prices** when demand is high, so some riders wait and more drivers come.

cards.q: In Design Uber, what happens to drivers who go silent, and how often does a parked driver send its location?
cards.a: We store when each driver last sent a location. Drivers not heard from in **30 seconds** (app closed, tunnel) are ignored, and a cleanup job removes them. A parked driver sends every **15 seconds**, not 30, so one late update won't make it blink out of the index.

cards.q: In Design Uber, how do you make sure a saved ride always reaches the matching queue?
cards.a: Save the ride **and** a "new ride request" outbox row in one transaction. An Outbox Relay sends the rows to Kafka. Saving, then sending, could crash in between and leave the ride `matching` forever. A request sent twice is fine: workers skip rides no longer `matching`.

cards.q: In a payment system, what does the quick math say, and what do we pick?
cards.a: 1 million a day ÷ about 100,000 seconds = about **10 payments per second**, so one normal **SQL database with transactions** is fine. We pick consistency over availability: better to say "please try again" than charge twice.

cards.q: In a payment system, how do card numbers stay off our servers?
cards.a: The buyer types the card number into the PSP's own form. The PSP gives back a **token**, a random stand-in that is useless to a thief. We only ever see the token, so most PCI DSS rules don't apply to us.

cards.q: In a payment system, where does the payment amount come from?
cards.a: From the server. The browser sends only the `orderId`, and the Payment Service reads the total from the Order Service. If the browser sent the amount, a buyer could change `2500` to `1`.

cards.q: In a payment system, how should money amounts be stored?
cards.a: As a whole number of cents: `2500` means $25.00. Never use decimal numbers (floats) for money. In most languages `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`.

cards.q: In a payment system, how do you make sure a customer is never charged twice?
cards.a: Use an **idempotency key** end to end. The client makes one key per payment attempt and sends it on every retry. A **unique** rule in our database lets only the first request create a payment, and we pass the same key to the PSP.

cards.q: In a payment system, why save the payment as `PENDING` before calling the PSP?
cards.a: If our server crashes in the middle, the row tells us a payment was in progress. A timeout means "we don't know yet". We retry with the same key, so the PSP returns the first result instead of charging again.

cards.q: In a payment system, why is "check for an existing payment first" not enough?
cards.a: Two requests can check at the exact same moment, both see no payment, and both charge. This is a race condition. Disabling the Pay button only stops double-clicks, not network retries or timeouts.

cards.q: In a payment system, a buyer presses Pay in two browser tabs. How do you stop two charges?
cards.a: Each tab makes its own idempotency key, so the key alone lets both through. A **partial unique index** allows only one `PENDING` or `SUCCEEDED` payment per order, so the second tab's insert fails.

cards.q: In a payment system, how do you handle a webhook from the PSP safely?
cards.a: **Check the signature**, made with a secret only the PSP and we know. **De-duplicate** by `eventId` with a unique rule, saved in the same transaction as the status update, so an event is never marked seen but not applied. Then find the payment by our own `paymentId`, sent as metadata.

cards.q: In a payment system, what is a double-entry ledger?
cards.a: Money never appears or disappears, it only moves. Every payment is written as at least two lines that add up to zero, like buyer −25.00, store +24.00, PSP fees +1.00. If the total is ever not zero, there is a bug.

cards.q: In a payment system, what three rules make the ledger trustworthy?
cards.a: **Append-only:** never update or delete a line. Fixes and refunds add new lines. **One transaction** for the status change and its lines. **Balances are sums** of the lines, and the lines are the truth.

cards.q: In a payment system, "succeeded" can arrive from the PSP, a webhook, the checker and reconciliation. How are ledger lines written only once?
cards.a: Only the `UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'PENDING'` that changes 1 row writes ledger lines. 0 rows means someone already did it, so roll back. A unique rule on `(source_id, account)` is a second lock on the door.

cards.q: In a payment system, how do you tell the Order Service a payment succeeded without losing the event?
cards.a: The **Outbox Pattern**: in the same transaction, write the event to an `outbox` table. A small relay reads that table and sends the events to Kafka. Saving and then sending could crash in between.

cards.q: In a payment system, what is reconciliation, and when does it run?
cards.a: Comparing our payments with the PSP's, line by line, and fixing every difference. Fast: a stuck-payment checker every few minutes. Slow but complete: a nightly job against the PSP's daily settlement report.

cards.q: In a payment system, the PSP is down. Which payments may switch to a second PSP?
cards.a: Only ones we know the first PSP did **not** charge, like when the connection was refused. A payment whose call timed out must stay `PENDING` with the first PSP, or the card could be charged twice.

cards.q: In a payment system, a $25.00 payment had a $1.00 PSP fee. How is a full refund written if the PSP keeps its fee?
cards.a: New lines with the refund's own `source_id`: buyer +25.00, store −25.00. The fee line is not reversed, so the refund costs the store the $1.00 fee. Nothing old is touched, and the lines still add up to zero.

cards.q: In a payment system, why not use a distributed transaction (2PC) with the PSP?
cards.a: The PSP is another company and will not join our database transaction. So we save `PENDING` first, call the PSP with an idempotency key, then save the result. The stuck-payment checker and reconciliation fix anything that breaks in between, like a saga.

cards.q: In a payment system, we crash after saving `PENDING` but before calling the PSP. What happens?
cards.a: A retry sees `PENDING` and calls the PSP again with the **same key**: safe, it charges at most once per key. If no retry comes, the checker finds no record at the PSP and, after a set time, marks it `FAILED`, so the buyer can pay again. Reconciliation refunds a late charge.

cards.q: In a payment system, how do you stop partial refunds from giving back more than was paid?
cards.a: Each refund first takes its share with one conditional update: `refunded_cents = refunded_cents + 1000` only if `refunded_cents + 1000 <= amount_cents`. 0 rows: refuse it. Two refunds at once can't both pass. The payment is `REFUNDED` once all of it is given back.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, what does the quick math say about the number of machines?
cards.a: Memory: 1 TB ÷ about 100 GB of data per machine = about **10 machines**. Traffic: 1 million ÷ about 100,000 requests per second per node = about **10** again. So the data must be split.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, what is inside one cache node, and how fast is a request?
cards.a: A **hash map in RAM**, which finds a key in about the same time no matter how many keys there are. Each entry stores the value and its expiry time. `GET` and `SET` take about 1 ms, including the network.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, why is `hash(key) % N` a bad way to pick a node?
cards.a: When N changes, almost every key moves. Going from 3 to 4 nodes moves about **75%** of keys, so most reads miss and all of them hit the database at once.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, how does consistent hashing pick a node?
cards.a: Nodes and keys sit on a **ring** of numbers, and a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node only moves the keys next to it: about **1/N** of them.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, what do virtual nodes give you?
cards.a: Each real machine sits at many spots on the ring. Keys spread more evenly, and when a machine dies, its keys are shared by many machines, not dumped on one neighbor.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, how are expired keys removed without checking every TTL all the time?
cards.a: **On read:** check the expiry, and if it has passed, delete the key and return "not found". **In the background:** a few times a second, check a small random set of keys with a TTL and delete the expired ones.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, which key do you evict when memory is full, and why?
cards.a: **LRU:** the key nobody has read for the longest time. Popular keys keep getting read, so they stay. FIFO might throw out the most popular key, and refusing new writes keeps fresh data out. Redis refuses writes by default (`noeviction`), so set `allkeys-lru`.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, how is LRU built so it stays fast?
cards.a: A **hash map** to find a key fast, plus a **list ordered by last use**. Every read moves the key to the newest end. When memory is full, remove from the oldest end.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, what is the best way to survive a node dying?
cards.a: Each **primary** has one or two **replicas**. When the primary stops answering, the coordination service promotes a replica within seconds and updates the cluster map. Manual failover takes minutes and needs someone awake.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, why is a lost `DELETE` worse than a lost `SET`?
cards.a: Replicas get copies in the background, so failover can lose the last few writes. A lost `SET` just causes a miss. A lost `DELETE` leaves the old value, so readers get stale data. So every key gets a **TTL**.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, how does failover avoid split brain?
cards.a: Failover is decided by **majority vote** in the coordination service. A primary takes writes only while it holds a **lease** it keeps renewing. The service waits longer than the lease before promoting, so the old primary has already stopped.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, how do you handle one very hot key?
cards.a: Keep it in a tiny **local cache** on each app server for a few seconds. Or store **copies** like `profile:1#1` to `profile:1#5`, which usually land on different nodes, and read a random one. On a change, update or delete every copy. Or **read from replicas**.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, a popular key expires and 10,000 requests miss at once. What do you do?
cards.a: This is a **cache stampede**. Let only one request rebuild the value, using a short lock, while the others wait a moment or get the old value. A small random amount added to each TTL stops keys expiring at the same second.

cards.q: In a distributed cache, how does Redis Cluster split keys, route clients and do failover?
cards.a: It splits keys into **16,384 hash slots**, and each primary owns a range. A node asked for a key it doesn't own answers `MOVED` with the right node. There is no separate coordination service: when a primary fails, a majority of the other primaries vote to promote one of its replicas.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, what does the quick math say?
cards.a: 1 million messages × 1 KB = **1 GB per second**. Kept 7 days, that is about **600 TB**, or about **1.8 PB** with 3 copies. So messages go on disk, split across many machines.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, what are topics, partitions and offsets?
cards.a: A **topic** is a named stream, like `orders`. It is split into **partitions**: ordered lists that only grow at the end. An **offset** is a message's position number in its partition: 0, 1, 2 ...

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, how does a producer choose a partition?
cards.a: With a key, it uses `hash(key) % partitions`, so the same key always goes to the same partition and stays in order. Without a key, it spreads messages evenly.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, why store each partition as an append-only log, not a database table?
cards.a: Disks are slow at random access but fast at sequential writes, and an append-only log only writes sequentially. A table updates indexes on every insert, and once one consumer deletes a message, no other service can read it.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, why split a partition into segment files?
cards.a: Only the newest segment gets new messages. When a segment is older than 7 days, we delete the **whole file** at once. That is much cheaper than deleting messages one by one.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, besides segments, what tricks make the log fast?
cards.a: A small **index** per segment, so a reader can jump straight to any offset. The OS **page cache**, so consumers that keep up read from memory. And **batches**: many messages sent and written to disk together.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, how can several services read the same messages without affecting each other?
cards.a: Each **consumer group** saves its own offset for each partition. Reading never deletes anything, so one group can be slow, or rewind and re-read old messages, without touching the others.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, how is the work shared inside one consumer group?
cards.a: The partitions are split among the group's consumers. **One partition is read by only one consumer in the group**, so its order is kept. With 4 partitions and 5 consumers, one sits idle: partitions limit parallelism.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, when should a consumer commit its offset?
cards.a: **After processing:** a crash means handling some messages again (at-least-once), so make consumers idempotent. Committing before processing is at-most-once: a crash can skip a message forever.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, how do you make sure a saved message is never lost?
cards.a: Keep each partition on **3 brokers**: a leader and two followers. With `acks = all`, the leader replies only after the in-sync followers have the message too. Add a rule like "at least 2 copies must be in sync".

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, why are `acks = 0` and `acks = 1` weaker than `acks = all`?
cards.a: With `acks = 0`, the producer never knows if the message arrived, so messages can be lost silently. With `acks = 1`, if the leader dies before any follower copied the message, it is lost.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, what happens when a partition's leader dies?
cards.a: A **controller**, a small group of servers that agree using a method like Raft, picks one of the **in-sync** followers as the new leader and tells everyone. Producers and consumers switch to it.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, why do consumers pull instead of the broker pushing?
cards.a: With pull, each consumer reads at its own speed, can rewind, and can grab big batches. With push, a slow consumer gets flooded. An idle consumer keeps asking, so use long polling: the broker holds the request open until there is data.

cards.q: In a distributed message queue, how is exactly-once possible inside the queue system?
cards.a: The broker gives each producer an **ID** and numbers its messages, so a retried send is spotted and not stored twice. A **transaction** saves the output messages and the consumer's new offset together, so both happen or neither does. It costs more than at-least-once.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, what is the difference between logs and metrics?
cards.a: **Logs** are text lines that describe one event: "what exactly happened to this order?" **Metrics** are numbers measured over time: "is something wrong right now, and since when?" Store them differently.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, what does the quick math say about logs?
cards.a: 10,000 servers × 100 lines per second × 200 bytes = **200 MB per second**: about 17 TB per day and 500 TB for 30 days. So we need hot and cold storage, and we must compress.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, what does the quick math say about metrics?
cards.a: 10,000 servers × 1,000 metrics = **10 million time series**. One reading every 10 seconds = **1 million numbers per second**. A normal SQL table would drown, so we need a time-series database.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, how do you collect logs from 10,000 servers without losing data?
cards.a: **Agent → Kafka → indexer workers.** An agent on each server sends batches to a thin Ingest Service, which puts them in Kafka. Indexers write to storage at a steady speed. Kafka absorbs the spike that comes with every outage.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, what does the agent do if the Ingest Service can't be reached?
cards.a: It saves batches to a **local disk buffer** and sends them later. If even that fills up, it drops `DEBUG` lines first and keeps `ERROR` lines.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, should metrics be pushed or pulled?
cards.a: Both work. **Push** (the agent sends, like StatsD) is good for short jobs and servers behind firewalls. **Pull** (a collector asks, like Prometheus) shows who is down: a failed pull means "server down".

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, how does a time-series database save space?
cards.a: It stores each series' points together in blocks and compresses them: timestamps as "same gap as before", values as how much they changed. **Downsampling** keeps less detail for old data, like 1-hour averages for a year.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, why should you never put user IDs in metric labels?
cards.a: Every new combination of labels creates a new time series. A `userId` label has millions of values (high **cardinality**), so it creates millions of series and can crash the TSDB. Put IDs in logs.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, how are logs stored as they get older?
cards.a: **Hot** (last 7 days): fast SSDs, fully indexed. **Warm** (7 to 30 days): cheaper disks. **Cold** (30 days to 1 year): compressed files in S3. Logs are split by day, so deleting old data is just dropping a whole index.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, how do you make log search fast?
cards.a: Every search **must** have a time range. Data is split by day and service, so a search opens only a tiny slice, and an index finds the matching lines inside it. Scanning every file would take hours.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, should you use a full-text index or a labels-only index?
cards.a: **Full-text** (an inverted index of every word) is very fast for any word, but big and CPU-heavy. **Labels-only** indexes service, level, host and time, then scans compressed chunks in parallel: much cheaper, but slower for one word everywhere.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, how do alerts avoid waking people for a 10-second blip?
cards.a: Rules have a "for" duration, like "more than 5% fail **for 5 minutes**". A broken rule goes from OK to PENDING. Only if it is still broken after 5 minutes does it go FIRING and page someone.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, besides the "for" duration, what makes alerts good?
cards.a: Alert on **metrics**, not logs. **Group** duplicates, so one outage sends one message, not 200 pages. **Route** each alert to the right team. And **watch the watcher** with a dead man's switch: an always-firing alert to an outside service.

cards.q: In a logging and metrics system, how is the work split over many machines?
cards.a: Every layer is partitioned. **Kafka:** many partitions, and the Ingest Service picks one by `hash(host)`. **Log store:** each day's index is split by service into shards. **TSDB:** series are spread by `hash(metric name + labels)`, so one series is one fast read.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, what does the quick math say, and what does it decide?
cards.a: 1 billion clicks ÷ 86,400 seconds = about **12,000 per second**, and about **30,000** at peak. `COUNT(*)` on every dashboard view would scan millions of rows, so we **count ahead of time**: one row per ad per minute.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, what happens when a user clicks an ad?
cards.a: The ad link points to our `/click` URL. The Click Service saves the click event to Kafka, waiting for all copies, **then** sends the user on with a `302` redirect. Redirecting first would lose the click if the service crashed.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, what is the best way to keep counts fast and fresh?
cards.a: **Stream processing.** Clicks go into Kafka, and Flink counts clicks per ad in **1-minute tumbling windows**: fixed buckets that don't overlap. When a minute ends, it writes the counts. Advertisers see them within seconds.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, why is an hourly batch job only "okay"?
cards.a: A batch job like Spark can count clicks per ad per minute into a fast database, so queries are fast. But the numbers are up to an hour old, and advertisers should see new clicks within about 1 minute.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, a click from 10:00:50 arrives at 10:01:20. Which minute does it count in?
cards.a: The 10:00 minute: we use **event time**, not arrival time. Each window stays open a little longer, say 30 seconds, tracked by a **watermark**. Clicks that come even later are fixed by the nightly batch job.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, where are the counts stored, and how do long-range charts stay fast?
cards.a: In an **OLAP database** like ClickHouse, Druid or Pinot, built for fast counts and sums over huge numbers of rows. **Rollups** keep per-hour and per-day totals, so a 90-day chart reads 90 rows, not 129,600.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, how do you stop a double-click from being counted twice?
cards.a: Each time an ad is shown, it gets a unique **impression ID**, signed so nobody can invent fake ones. The stream processor remembers which impression IDs it has seen today and ignores repeats.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, how do checkpoints stop double counting after the stream processor crashes?
cards.a: Every few seconds, Flink saves its running counts and its Kafka position **together**. After a crash, it loads the snapshot and re-reads Kafka from that position. The counts were rolled back too, so each click counts once.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, why write "set to 42" instead of "add 42"?
cards.a: Results can be written twice after a restart. "Set" is safe to repeat: the same write twice gives the same result. "Add" would count those clicks twice.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, what gives the final numbers used for billing?
cards.a: An S3 sink, a second Kafka consumer, copies every raw click to S3. Every night a **batch job recounts** the day and fixes any differences. Billing uses the recount. Fast stream plus slow batch is the **Lambda architecture**.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, how do you handle a hot ad that floods one Kafka partition?
cards.a: Add a suffix to its key, like `ad_1:0` to `ad_1:9`, so its clicks spread over 10 partitions. Each worker counts its part, and a small second step adds the 10 parts together.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, why must the hot-ad suffix be `hash(impressionId) % 10`, not random?
cards.a: Dedupe happens inside each worker. With a random suffix, two copies of one impression could land on different workers, and each counts it once. With the hash, the copies always meet in the same worker.

cards.q: In an ad click aggregator, which numbers must be exact, and which can be approximate?
cards.a: Clicks for billing are money, so they must be **exact**. "How many different users clicked?" can be approximate: a **HyperLogLog** estimates unique items with tiny, fixed memory, usually off by only about 1%.

cards.q: In Design Top K, what does the quick math say?
cards.a: Exact counts need 1 billion videos × about 16 bytes = about **16 GB** per window, and sorting a billion numbers every minute is far too slow. So split the counting across machines and keep only the top K.

cards.q: In Design Top K, how do you find the top K without sorting everything?
cards.a: Use a **min-heap of size K**, which always shows its smallest item. Go through the counts: if one is bigger than the heap's smallest, swap them. The heap only ever holds K items.

cards.q: In Design Top K, how do you count 100,000 views per second?
cards.a: Kafka splits view events **by video ID**, so all views of one video go to one worker. Each worker counts its own videos and keeps its own top K. A merger combines the small lists into the global top K.

cards.q: In Design Top K, why must views be split by video ID, never randomly?
cards.a: With one worker per video, a global top-100 video must be in its worker's top 100, so merging local lists is correct. Split randomly, a video could be number 101 on every worker and never appear, though it is number 1 overall.

cards.q: In Design Top K, a viral video gets 5% of all views. Why is one worker for it still fine?
cards.a: That is about 5,000 tiny events per second, and adding 1 in memory can be done millions of times a second. If it were ever too much, the View Ingest servers would pre-count per second before Kafka, sending events like `v_981: +350`.

cards.q: In Design Top K, how do you keep a "last hour" count without recounting?
cards.a: Count views per video per **minute** and keep a running total. Each minute, add the newest minute and subtract the minute that just fell out of the window. Example: 500 + 40 − 25 = 515.

cards.q: In Design Top K, what bucket sizes do the last-hour, last-day and all-time windows use?
cards.a: Last hour: 1-minute buckets, keep 60. Last day: 1-hour buckets, keep 24. All time: no buckets, just one running total.

cards.q: In Design Top K, how does a Count-Min Sketch add and read counts?
cards.a: It is a small fixed table, with one hash function per row. To add a view, add 1 in the column each row's hash picks. To read a count, take the **smallest** of the video's cells across all rows.

cards.q: In Design Top K, what are the strengths and limits of a Count-Min Sketch?
cards.a: It never counts too low, only sometimes a little too high, and its size stays the same for a thousand or a billion videos. But it can't list videos, so pair it with a min-heap of size K.

cards.q: In Design Top K, why does the sketch-plus-heap trick break for "last hour"?
cards.a: It only works when counts only go up. In a sliding window counts go down, but the heap only hears about a video on a new view. A video that went quiet would stay in the heap with its old, high count.

cards.q: In Design Top K, how do you use Count-Min Sketches for a sliding window?
cards.a: Keep one small sketch per minute bucket, with the same hash functions, and add and subtract them for a running last-hour sketch. Keep candidates: the top few thousand videos of each recent minute. Every minute, rebuild the heap from scratch.

cards.q: In Design Top K, how do the nightly batch and the stream share the all-time list?
cards.a: Only the merger writes the lists people read. The batch writes a **base** into its own table: exact all-time counts up to a **cut-off time** (midnight). The merger adds the stream count since that cut-off. Until the new base arrives, it keeps the old base and its older cut-off, so no hour is lost.

cards.q: In Design Top K, how do reads stay fast?
cards.a: Reads never count. Every minute, the merger writes the top 1,000 for each window to Redis as one small value, and `k=100` takes the first 100. A CDN or a short cache in front can serve almost every request.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, what is the hard part, and why is no quick math needed?
cards.a: The hard part is **edits at the same time**, not scale. Documents are small and each edit is a few bytes. The goal is **convergence**: after all edits arrive, every copy of the document is identical.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, why use a WebSocket for live editing?
cards.a: Live editing needs messages in both directions: my edits go up, and everyone else's come down. A WebSocket stays open and lets the server push messages at any time. We send small ops, not the whole document.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, why does the browser open the WebSocket with `fromVersion`?
cards.a: Someone may type between `GET /docs/d_42` and the WebSocket opening. The server first sends every op after that version, then the live ops. So nothing is missed, and this copy doesn't differ from everyone else's.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, the doc says `CAT`. Alice inserts H at 1, Bob deletes position 2. What goes wrong?
cards.a: If each applies the other's edit as sent, Alice ends with `CHT` and Bob with `CHA`. The copies differ. On Alice's screen, her `H` pushed the `T` to position 3, so she lost the wrong letter.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, how does Operational Transformation (OT) fix crossing edits?
cards.a: It **adjusts one edit** so it still means what its author meant. A central server decides the order and transforms ops: after Alice's insert at 1, Bob's "delete 2" becomes "delete 3". Everyone ends with `CHA`.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, why must each browser also transform the ops it receives?
cards.a: Its own unconfirmed edits are already on screen. So it transforms each op from the server against all its **pending** ops (the one in flight, then the buffer), and updates them the same way. It keeps only **one op in flight**: later typing waits in a buffer until that op is confirmed.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, how is a CRDT different from OT?
cards.a: A CRDT gives every character a **fixed unique ID**, so edits like "insert H after `c1`" work in any order on any copy. No central server is needed and offline editing is natural, but it uses more memory: an ID per character, plus tombstones.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, why pick OT over CRDTs for this design?
cards.a: We already have a server for every document, and OT keeps memory small. Google Docs uses OT. If offline editing becomes important, CRDTs are the better fit.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, how do all editors of one document reach the same server?
cards.a: Use **consistent hashing** on the document ID to choose its **owner server**. The load balancer sends every WebSocket for that doc to the owner, which orders its ops. A coordination service like ZooKeeper keeps the list of servers.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, how do you stop two servers that both think they own a doc from splitting its history?
cards.a: A **fence** in the ops log. Each entry's key is `(doc_id, version)`, and an append succeeds only if that version is still free. So only one server can write version 1288, and the history stays one straight line.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, what happens when a document's owner server dies?
cards.a: Its documents move to the next server on the ring, which loads the snapshot plus recent ops. Browsers reconnect with `fromVersion` and resend the op never confirmed. Each op has an ID like `c7f3a-17` (the tab's client ID plus a counter), so a copy already saved is ignored.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, how is a document saved and opened?
cards.a: Every op is appended to an **operations log**. After every 1,000 ops or so, a worker saves a **snapshot** of the full text. Open = load the latest snapshot, then replay the newer ops. The author hears "saved" only after the log write.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, how do you show who is online and where their cursors are?
cards.a: Presence lives **in memory** on the owner server, never in the database. Users are removed when their WebSocket closes or no heartbeat comes for about 30 seconds. A lost cursor move is not retried: the next one fixes it.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, how do undo and version restore work?
cards.a: **Undo** only your own last op: make the opposite op, then transform it against everything others did since. **Restore** never deletes history: rebuild the old version (snapshot + replay), then add new ops that turn the current text into it.

cards.q: In Design Google Docs, why does each browser keep only one op in flight?
cards.a: If Alice sends `H` at 1 and `E` at 2, both based on 1287, the server transforms `E` against her own `H` and moves it to 3: `CHAET`, not `CHEAT`. So `E` waits in a buffer until `H` is confirmed, then goes out based on 1288. The server only transforms against other people's ops.
